# Plan Your Weekly Meals and Shopping List with Any AI Assistant

By the end of this guide, you'll have a five-day dinner plan and a ready-to-shop shopping list — written in your words, for your family. This works with any AI assistant (think ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or DeepSeek), so use whichever one you already have an account with.

## Before you start

- **An AI assistant** you can type into — a free account with ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek, or a similar tool is fine. Both the website and the mobile app work.
- **Roughly 10–15 minutes** to answer the AI's follow-up questions and tweak the plan.
- **A pen and paper, or your phone's notes app**, to copy the final list.
- **No paid plan is required** for this task on any of the assistants listed above. If you want to save the chat history, you may need a free sign-in.
- One honest heads-up: the AI can **draft** a plan and a list, but it can't taste your food, check your fridge, or place a grocery order for you. You'll do the cooking and the shopping yourself — the AI just makes the thinking part quicker.

## Step 1 — Open your AI assistant and start a new chat

Open the website or app of the AI you use, and start a **fresh, empty chat**. Think of a chat like a blank page in a notebook — the AI only remembers what you write in *this* conversation, so starting clean keeps things tidy. You'll see a text box at the bottom (or middle) of the screen with a prompt like *"Message ChatGPT"* or *"Ask Gemini"*. If you don't see that box, look for a **+** or **New chat** button — usually at the top of a sidebar on the left, or behind a pencil icon.

💬 Example: don't type anything yet — just make sure you can see the empty text box.

You'll know it worked when the screen shows a blank conversation with your name at the top and a blinking cursor in the message box.

## Step 2 — Tell the AI about your household in one message

In that empty text box, **type one short message describing your family**. The more concrete you are, the better the plan you'll get back. Mention the number of people eating, any allergies or foods you avoid (gluten, nuts, dairy, pork, shellfish — whatever applies), and roughly how much you'd like to spend per week. If you have a slow cooker, an air fryer, or only one working hob, mention that too — it changes the suggestions.

💬 Example: *"Family of four in Sydney: two adults, a hungry 14-year-old, and a 7-year-old who won't eat spicy food. No nuts or shellfish. One of us is vegetarian most nights. Budget around $120 AUD for five dinners. We have an oven and a stovetop, no microwave."*

You'll know it worked when the AI replies by **summarizing back what you told it** and asking one or two clarifying questions. If it just says "Sure, what would you like?" — that's a sign your message was too short, so add a few more details and send it again.

## Step 3 — Ask for the five-day dinner plan

Now **send a follow-up asking specifically for a five-night dinner plan**. Use the word "dinner" rather than "meal" so the AI doesn't accidentally add breakfast or lunch. Ask it to keep each recipe under 30 minutes, to repeat ingredients across nights where it makes sense (so you cook once and re-use), and to flag any night that needs you to **soak, marinate, or defrost something in advance**. If it looks different on your device and the AI offers bullet points, that's fine — just read them in order.

💬 Example: *"Great, thanks. Please give me a five-night dinner plan based on that. Keep each dinner under 30 minutes of active cooking, repeat ingredients across nights where it makes sense (saves money and waste), and call out any night that needs overnight prep like defrosting or marinating."*

You'll know it worked when the AI responds with a numbered list of five dinners, each with a short ingredient list and a rough time estimate. If a recipe uses something obscure or expensive, the AI usually notes it — read that note before moving on.

## Step 4 — Ask for the matching shopping list

Reply in the same chat and **ask the AI to turn the plan into a single shopping list, grouped by aisle**. Grouping by aisle (produce, meat, pantry, dairy, frozen) saves you real time in the supermarket because you walk through the shop once instead of zig-zagging. Also ask it to **include rough amounts** (e.g. "500g chicken mince", "1 brown onion") so you can compare prices, and to **note anything you probably already have** — olive oil, salt, pepper, plain flour. If your AI's reply comes back as a wall of text, just reply "Could you put that as a bullet list grouped by aisle?" and it will reformat.

💬 Example: *"Nice plan. Can you turn that into one shopping list grouped by aisle (produce, meat/fridge, pantry, dairy, frozen) with rough amounts? And please mark staples I likely already have at home — oil, salt, pepper, basic spices — so I don't have to buy them."*

You'll know it worked when you see a clean, aisle-grouped list with amounts beside each item, and a short "you probably already have" note at the end. If anything is unclear (like "some herbs" instead of "a small bunch of parsley"), reply and ask for specifics — the AI is happy to be more precise.

## Step 5 — Personalize and stress-test the plan

Read through the list with a **"will my family actually eat this?"** eye. This is the step most people skip, and it's where a plan either succeeds or ends up half-eaten. Reply with any swaps you want — *"swap the salmon for chicken thighs"*, *"the kids won't eat couscous, can we have rice instead?"* — and ask the AI to **re-output the updated shopping list**. This is also a good moment to ask it to check for **duplicate ingredients** across the week (buying one bunch of coriander and using it three ways is cheaper than buying three).

💬 Example: *"Looks good but please swap the salmon for chicken thighs (cheaper this week), change the couscous to jasmine rice, and double-check I'm not buying the same herb or spice twice across the five nights. Then re-print the shopping list."*

You'll know it worked when the AI gives you a revised plan *and* a revised list, and you can see that the changes actually flowed through. If the old salmon is still on the list, point that out and ask for another pass.

## Step 6 — Save the list where you'll see it on shopping day

Finally, **copy the shopping list out of the chat and into a place you'll actually look at it**. The AI can't push the list to your phone's Reminders app for you, so this last step is on you. Most people either screenshot the list, paste it into their phone's Notes app, or write it on the back of an envelope. While you're at it, copy the five dinners into a separate note titled "This week's dinners" and stick it on the fridge — it stops the 5pm *"what's for dinner?"* panic.

💬 Example: a quick message you can send to yourself or a family member: *"Here are this week's dinners: Mon – chicken stir-fry, Tue – veggie pasta, Wed – sheet-pan sausages and veg, Thu – rice bowl with leftover chicken, Fri – omelette night. Shopping list attached."*

You'll know it worked when the list is in your pocket, your fridge, or your phone — anywhere you'll actually see it before you walk into the shop. If the AI's formatting was messy, just tidy it as you copy.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for "a meal plan" without saying "dinner".** The AI often defaults to three meals a day, which is overwhelming. Always specify *"dinner"* (or breakfast, or lunches) so the list stays useful.
- **Forgetting to mention one dietary need.** A single missed allergy can ruin a whole week. Before you press send, re-read your message and check: did I mention all allergies, all the fussy eaters, and all the equipment I actually have?
- **Trusting the first list without stress-testing it.** The AI doesn't know your family's taste buds. If a recipe sounds like something they'd refuse, swap it now in Step 5 — not at 5:30pm when you're starving and the kids are hungry.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** You skip the Sunday-afternoon "what should we eat?" spiral, walk into the supermarket knowing exactly what to grab, and throw away less food because the plan repeats ingredients on purpose.
- **For your business or work:** The same prompt-writing habit transfers anywhere — drafting meeting agendas, planning a project, or organizing a trip. Once you've practiced telling an AI *who you are, what you need, and what to avoid*, you can use that pattern everywhere.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't worry about getting the prompt perfect on the first try. The AI is patient — if its first answer isn't quite right, just say *"close, but please change X"* and it'll try again. That's the whole trick.

## Try it now

Open your AI assistant right now and paste this single message to get started:

> *"I'm a family of [number] in [your city]. We need a five-night dinner plan on a budget of $[X] AUD. We don't eat [allergies or foods to avoid]. Please keep each dinner under 30 minutes, repeat ingredients across nights, and tell me what to defrost the night before."*

Reply to whatever it gives you, ask for the shopping list, and you're done. Ten minutes tonight, five relaxed dinners next week.
